props.name: multiple
props.description: Whether several panels may be open at once. When false, opening one item closes the others.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual dressing. `default` is the stroked container with a hard shadow; `plain` drops the container chrome for an accordion that sits inside a card — mirror of sk-card's `bare` reasoning.

props.name: heading
props.description: The summary text.  A `<span>` inside the `<summary>`, not a heading element: the item does not know what level it sits at in the document outline, and a hard-coded heading inside it contradicts the surrounding structure (sk-card's stated reason for the same shape).

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the panel is expanded. Mirrors `<details open>` and is reflected: a consumer can author `<sk-accordion-item open>` in HTML — including server-rendered markup for an already-expanded item — and the attribute tracks what the browser did on a user toggle, so the parent can close siblings and the consumer can read the real state.

ai.summary: A stack of disclosure panels where one, or several, can be open at a time.
whenToUse: Secondary content belongs on the page but should not occupy it — questions, advanced settings, release notes
The reader opens panels in any order and may want none of them open
The content is short enough to expand in place rather than to open a route
whenNotToUse: The sections are the page's navigation — use Tabs
The content must be read in order, or hiding it loses the thread — keep it on the page
Every panel starts open and none should close — use headings and sections
ai.accessibility: Built on the native `<details>` and `<summary>` elements, so the disclosure semantics, the focus stop, the expanded state, and Enter and Space are the browser's rather than reimplemented — which is why the item needs no ARIA of its own. The marker is aria-hidden and drawn with pseudo-elements. `heading` renders as a span inside the summary; a consumer that needs a real heading level puts one in the slot. The summary meets `--sk-touch-min`.
ai.example:

No.
knownLimitations: Exclusive by default: opening an item closes its siblings, and `multiple` opts out
No group-level event summarises the open items — each item dispatches its own bubbling `sk-open-change` with `detail.open`

props.name: initialFocus
props.description: Selector or element id for the control that receives initial focus — the action the consumer wants to be the default. Falls back to the first button in the panel.

props.name: label
props.description: Accessible name. Required in spirit: an interruption that announces nothing is a modal mystery. Prefer a real heading in the `title` slot.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the alert is showing.

ai.summary: A forced decision on the glass material: role=alertdialog, no Escape, no backdrop click — the user must choose an action.
whenToUse: The action is destructive and irreversible — a delete, a revoke, a permanent change
The page cannot continue until the question is answered
The interruption must be announced as an interruption, not as a window
whenNotToUse: The user may reasonably decline without answering — use a Dialog, which allows Escape and optional backdrop dismissal
The message is informational and needs no decision — use a Toast or Alert
The action has a URL or needs deep linking — use a page
ai.accessibility: `role="alertdialog"`, so assistive technology announces an interruption rather than a window. Escape is *refused* and the backdrop does not dismiss: a dialog that lets Escape answer its question did not need to be asked — this is the ARIA APG's requirement for the role, not a style choice. Focus lands on `initialFocus` (the consumer's chosen default action) rather than the first focusable, because in a delete confirmation the wrong default is a destructive one. Label it with a real heading in the `title` slot. The panel wears the danger stroke: an interruption should look like one before a single word is read.

knownLimitations: There is no trigger slot: the application raises it in response to something, never the user browsing
There is no imperative `close()` without a decision — the only exit is an action

props.name: heading
props.description: Heading text for the alert, rendered as a `<span>`.  Named `heading`, not `title`, for the reason sk-card records: `title` is a standardized `HTMLElement` member and a prop by that name is shadowed by the prototype property, so the browser would surface it as a hover tooltip on the whole alert.  A string rather than a heading element: the alert does not know what level it sits at in the document's outline, and a hard-coded heading inside it produces a level that may contradict the surrounding structure. A consumer who needs a real heading puts one in the body itself.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.  Only `variant` is an appearance prop. The variant also picks the component's default live-region role, unless the consumer has already set one.

ai.summary: An inline message about the current page: a success, a warning, a failure, or a note.
whenToUse: A result or a state needs stating next to the content it describes
A page-level or form-level failure must be visible without a modal
The message may need an action, such as Retry or View logs
whenNotToUse: It interrupts a flow the user must acknowledge — use an Alert Dialog
It is a transient, self-dismissing update — use a Toast
It labels a value with one word's worth of state — use a Badge
ai.accessibility: Carries `role="alert"` for the danger and warning variants, so those interrupt; the rest are `role="status"` and wait for a pause. The variant glyph is aria-hidden and differs in shape as well as colour, so the message survives a monochrome display. A consumer-set `role` is never overwritten.
ai.example: <sk-alert variant="warning" heading="Quota nearly full">Your workspace is using 96% of its quota.</sk-alert>
knownLimitations: No dismiss control, deliberately: a dismissible alert needs focus management and a close affordance that belongs to a Dialog or a Toast
The actions slot is not part of the announced message, so an action the user must take also needs to exist in the page

ai.summary: A centred sign-in card: an email and password field, a remember-me checkbox, a submit button, a recovery link, and an error alert.
whenToUse: A sign-in, sign-up, or password-reset screen that needs the card, the fields, and the error state
You want the error alert and the recovery link placed where a user looks for them
whenNotToUse: An in-app login dialog — use Alert Dialog
A settings screen for an already signed-in user — use the settings block
ai.accessibility: The card is a single `<form>` with an accessible name from its heading; each field is labelled by a `<sk-label>` bound to it, and the password field declares `autocomplete="current-password"` so password managers and assistive technology recognise it. The error alert is a live region placed before the fields, and the recovery link is a real link rather than a button styled as one.
knownLimitations: Nothing is submitted and nothing is validated: the error alert demonstrates the state, it is not wired to a response
There is no second-factor step, no OAuth buttons, and no password-strength meter

props.name: dot
props.description: Renders the badge as a dot instead of a pill. Requires a text label for screen readers, because the dot itself conveys nothing but color.

props.name: size
props.description: Control height.

props.name: statusLabel
props.description: Screen-reader text for the dot variant. Required when `dot` is set.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.

ai.summary: A static label for status, category, or count. It is not interactive.
whenToUse: It marks a record's state, such as Active, Pending, or Failed
It labels a category or count that must stand out from body copy
It marks an item in a dense list where state has to stay scannable
whenNotToUse: It is clickable — use a Button, because a badge has no interaction
It navigates — use a Link instead
It carries a value the reader selects — use a Checkbox or Switch instead
ai.accessibility: Static text, so it exposes no role and no tab stop. Each variant sets a foreground and a background measured together, so the label clears 4.5:1 against its own fill rather than only against the page. The dot variant would otherwise convey state by color alone, which WCAG 1.4.1 forbids, so it renders the consumer-supplied `statusLabel` visually hidden instead.
knownLimitations: The `statusLabel` prop is required in the React types for the `dot` variant but only warns in plain HTML

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables interaction. Mirrors the ARIA name.

props.name: loading
props.description: Shows a busy state and blocks interaction.

props.name: size
props.description: Control height.

props.name: type
props.description: `submit`, `reset`, or `button`. Native semantics, so a Button inside a form behaves like the `<button>` a consumer would have written by hand.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.

props.name: form
props.description: The `id` of a `<form>` element to associate this element with.

props.name: name
props.description: The name of the element, used when submitting an HTML form.

ai.summary: Triggers an action: submit a form, open a dialog, save a change.
whenToUse: The control performs an action on the current page
It submits or resets a form
It opens a panel, dialog, or menu
whenNotToUse: It navigates somewhere — use a Link instead
It toggles a value on its own, with no action — use a Checkbox or Switch
It is the only option in a set — use a Radio Group
ai.accessibility: Button role. Activates on Enter and Space. A loading button is aria-busy rather than disabled, so it keeps its accessible name and position in the tab order.
knownLimitations: As a form-associated custom element, `type="submit"` calls form.requestSubmit() explicitly; native implicit submission does not apply

props.name: heading
props.description: Heading text for the card, rendered in the header.  Named `heading`, not `title`. `title` is a standardized `HTMLElement` member, and a prop by that name shadows the prototype property, so the browser would show this text as a hover tooltip on the entire card — a second, invisible copy of the heading appearing on hover. Stencil warns about this by name.  A string rather than a heading element: the card does not know what level it sits at in the document's outline, and a hard-coded `<h3>` inside a card in an `<h2>` section produces a heading level that contradicts the surrounding structure. A consumer who needs a real heading passes one in the `header` slot instead.

props.name: padding
props.description: The card's inner padding.  Not the `size` prop, because `size` is the height scale every other component uses and a card has no intrinsic height: it is whatever its content makes it. Padding is the axis a card actually varies on.

props.name: subtitle
props.description: Supporting text under the heading.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.  `default` is the raised, hard-edged surface every other chrome component matches. `outlined` drops the fill for a card that sits inside another surface, where two competing fills would fight. `bare` drops the shadow too, for a card that is grouped rather than elevated.

ai.summary: A hard-edged surface that groups related content, with optional header, body, and footer.
whenToUse: A group of related facts, settings, or actions needs a boundary of its own
Content sits inside another surface and needs a raised panel to read against it
A record needs a title, a body, and a row of actions below a rule
whenNotToUse: The whole card is one action — use a Button or a Link with card styling
You are nesting it inside another card to group further — two competing fills and shadows read as noise
The separation is a list of peers — use a plain list or a Separator
ai.accessibility: A card is a surface, not a control: it exposes no role, is not focusable, and has no interaction props, because a clickable card is a link or a button wearing a card's styling and adding a click handler here would produce something neither keyboard-reachable nor announced. `heading` renders as a `<span>`, not a heading, because the card does not know its level in the document outline — pass a real `<h2 slot="header">` when you need one. Slots are optional and each renders nothing when empty, so a card without a header carries no empty bordered band.
knownLimitations: There is no `size` prop: a card has no intrinsic height to scale, so `padding` is the axis it varies on
There is no click handler, by design — a card that navigates should be a Link, and one that acts should be a Button

props.name: checked
props.description: Whether the box is checked. An ARIA-mirroring boolean, so the ARIA name verbatim (ADR-013, decision 1) — not `isChecked`, not `value`.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Initial state for the uncontrolled case.

props.name: description
props.description: Persistent helper text below the row.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables interaction. Mirrors the ARIA name.

props.name: error
props.description: The validation message. Its presence drives `aria-invalid`.

props.name: form
props.description: Associates the control with a form it is not nested inside.

props.name: indeterminate
props.description: Visual "some children" state. Property-only on the platform — there is no `indeterminate` attribute — so this prop writes the DOM node after render and never reaches the form: an indeterminate box submits as unchecked.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Marks the field invalid, with the same independence from `error` as Input.

props.name: label
props.description: The label text, rendered beside the box. Wraps the control.

props.name: required
props.description: Native constraint validation still applies and is never suppressed.

props.name: size
props.description: Label text size. The row target stays 44px at every size.

props.name: value
props.description: The submitted value when checked. `"on"` is the platform default, kept so a plain form reads exactly what a native checkbox would send.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.

props.name: name
props.description: The name of the element, used when submitting an HTML form.

ai.summary: A boolean toggle that participates in a plain HTML form. Validation is the browser's, not this component's.
whenToUse: The value is a single yes/no choice that submits with a form
It must work without JavaScript: plain HTML form submission
The browser's native constraint validation is wanted — required means required
whenNotToUse: The choice is one of several exclusive options — use a Radio Group
It represents an on/off state that acts immediately without form submission — use a Switch
The value is text — use an Input or Textarea
ai.accessibility: Renders a real native `<input type="checkbox">`, so the browser supplies constraint validation, Space-to-toggle, and autofill rather than this component reimplementing them. The label wraps the input, making the whole row the activation target with no click handler. `label`, `description`, and `error` are wired through the wrapping label and `aria-describedby`; an error sets `aria-invalid` and renders an icon beside its text, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1). `indeterminate` is visual only (`aria-checked="mixed"`), and submits as unchecked. Implements the FACE contract: formResetCallback, formDisabledCallback, formStateRestoreCallback, and sk-value-change fires only for user-initiated changes.
ai.example: <sk-checkbox name="agree" label="I agree to the terms" required></sk-checkbox>
knownLimitations: The generated `id` for the inner control differs from React's `useId()`, so an SSR consumer must pass an explicit `id` for a separately-rendered `Label` to find it (section 4, forms contract)
`indeterminate` is a property, not an attribute — it cannot be set in declarative HTML and resets on re-render if not re-applied

ai.summary: An application shell with a navigation sidebar, a search header, summary cards, and a table of recent activity.
whenToUse: The first screen of an internal tool, where the shell matters more than any one panel
You want the layout, the sidebar behaviour, and the responsive breakpoints already settled
whenNotToUse: It is a marketing page — use Button and link components, not the sidebar shell
You only need the summary cards — take Card and write the grid yourself
ai.accessibility: The block is plain markup: the landmarks are the ones it writes (`<header>`, `<nav aria-label>`, `<main>`, `<section aria-labelledby>`), and the table carries a `<caption>`. Nothing in the block is keyboard-reachable that is not also labelled; the sidebar's links are real `<sk-link>` elements wrapping real `<a href>`, so they are in the tab order as links rather than as clickable boxes.
knownLimitations: The rows, counts, and progress values are placeholder markup: the block fetches nothing
The sidebar is not collapsible and the block ships no JavaScript to make it so

props.name: dismissible
props.description: Closes when the backdrop is clicked. Off by default because a dialog holding form input loses work to a stray click; a confirmation prompt with nothing to lose wants it on.

props.name: label
props.description: The dialog's accessible name, applied to the panel when the consumer has not slotted a `<sk-text>` heading. Prefer the slot: a real heading is visible to everyone and doubles as the label.

props.name: modal
props.description: Modal is the default and the usual case: the page behind is inert and the focus is trapped. Non-modal (Chrome/Edge/Firefox only — Safari has no `showModal`-independent backdrop) renders the panel inline without blocking the page, for tool-palette-style UIs.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the dialog is showing. Reflects so page CSS can target it.

props.name: showModal
props.description: Imperative open/close for non-template consumers. The props stay the declarative path; these exist because some callers (a toast-style flow) want to open without re-rendering.

ai.summary: A modal overlay on the glass material: focus is trapped by the native <dialog>, Escape closes, and focus returns to the invoker.
whenToUse: A decision must block the page until it is made — a confirmation, a discard warning
A short form needs the page's context hidden, not merely behind
Content must interrupt without navigating — use a page for anything that needs a URL
whenNotToUse: Content is supplementary and the page should stay live — use a Popover or Toast
The flow has its own URL or needs deep linking — use a page
It is a non-blocking status update — use a Toast
ai.accessibility: Renders the native `<dialog>` element: focus trapping, Escape, and inert background content are the browser's, not reimplemented. Focus returns to the invoker on close, so a keyboard user is not dropped at the top of the document. Label it with a real heading in the `title` slot — it is visible to everyone and doubles as the dialog's accessible name. One `sk-open-change` event reports every close path: trigger, Escape, backdrop, and a consumer setting the prop. The backdrop is translucent ink, not blur — the glass panel already blurs what is under it. `dismissible` is off by default: a dialog holding form input loses work to a stray click.

knownLimitations: The native `<dialog>` element is Baseline-tier: Core-tier browsers get the non-modal degradation, not the modal
Slotted content is moved into the panel once at upgrade — content added to the host after upgrade is not distributed

props.name: description
props.description: Supporting text under the heading.

props.name: heading
props.description: Plain text in a `<span>`, not a heading element. This component does not know what level it sits at in the document's outline, and a hard-coded heading inside it contradicts the surrounding structure. Decision shared with sk-card.

props.name: size
props.description: Density axis: block padding and glyph size. `md` is the default because an empty state usually fills the whole area left by the missing content.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual treatment.  `default` is the stroked, shadowed surface. `bare` drops the fill, the stroke and the shadow for an empty state nested inside another surface, where two competing boundaries would fight.

ai.summary: The surface a list, table, or panel shows when it has nothing to display.
whenToUse: A region is legitimately empty and the page should say why
The empty region has a next action, such as Create or Import
A filter or a search matched nothing and the user can widen it
whenNotToUse: The content is still loading — use a Skeleton or a Spinner
The message is about the page as a whole — use an Alert
It is a placeholder for one field inside a form
ai.accessibility: Not focusable, with no role and no live region: an empty state is content, not a status change, and announcing "no results" on every render is noise. `heading` renders as a span rather than a heading element, because the level belongs to the consumer's document outline — put a real heading in the body slot when it needs to be one. Slotted actions keep their own semantics.
ai.example:
<sk-empty-state heading="No deploys yet" description="Push to main and the first build starts on its own.">
  <sk-button slot="actions">New deploy</sk-button>
</sk-empty-state>
knownLimitations: `bare` drops the fill, the border, and the shadow rather than restyling them, because it exists for one inside a Card
The icon slot falls back to a dashed CSS glyph: this package ships no icon set

ai.summary: A square, icon-only control for actions that need no label, such as edit or delete.
whenToUse: The action is unambiguous from a well-known icon
Space is tight, such as a toolbar or a table row
The control sits next to a labelled control that implies the group
whenNotToUse: The action is not obvious from the icon alone — use a Button with a label
It is the primary or most common action on the page — use a Button
It performs navigation — use a Link instead

knownLimitations: The `label` prop is required in the React types but only warns in plain HTML

props.name: autocomplete
props.description: Autocomplete hint for the browser and password managers.

props.description: Initial value for the uncontrolled case.

props.description: Persistent helper text below the field.

props.description: Disables interaction. Mirrors the ARIA name.

props.name: error
props.description: The validation message. Its presence drives `aria-invalid`.

props.name: form
props.description: Associates the control with a form it is not nested inside.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Marks the field invalid.  Separate from `error` on purpose: a field can be invalid before the consumer knows why, and an error message can be present without the field being in an error state — for example a form-level summary listing several fields.

props.name: label
props.description: The control's own label text, rendered above the field.

props.name: maxLength
props.description: Maximum accepted length, enforced natively.

props.name: minLength
props.description: Minimum accepted length, enforced natively.

props.description: Makes the field non-editable but still submitted and focusable.  Attribute-observed, unlike `disabled`: the HTML attribute name is `readonly` in every case, so Stencil's camelCase-to-kebab mapping cannot be relied on to match it, and a consumer writing `<sk-input readonly>` in plain HTML was silently getting an editable field.

props.name: required
props.description: Native constraint validation still applies and is never suppressed.

props.name: size
props.description: Control height.

props.name: type
props.description: Native input type. Visual configuration stays `variant`/`size` only.

props.name: value
props.description: The value. Uncontrolled by default: typed value only if set.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.

props.name: name
props.description: The name of the element, used when submitting an HTML form.

ai.summary: A single-line text field that participates in a plain HTML form. Validation is the browser's, not this component's.
whenToUse: The value is a short string: a name, an email, a handle, a search term
It must submit through a plain `<form>` with no JavaScript state
The browser's own constraint validation is wanted rather than a bespoke rules engine
whenNotToUse: The value is long-form text — use a Textarea
The value is one of a fixed set — use a Select or Radio Group
It only toggles a boolean — use a Checkbox or Switch
ai.accessibility: Renders a real native `<input>`, so the browser supplies constraint validation, password managers, autofill, and IME composition rather than this component reimplementing them. `label`, `description`, and `error` are wired through `<label for>` and `aria-describedby`; an error also sets `aria-invalid` and renders an icon beside its text, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1). `readOnly` keeps the value submitted and focusable, which is what distinguishes it from `disabled`.
knownLimitations: The generated `id` for the inner control differs from React's `useId()`, so an SSR consumer must pass an explicit `id` for a separately-rendered `Label` to find it (section 4, forms contract)
The `pattern` prop takes a string, not a RegExp, because it becomes a native attribute

props.name: forId
props.description: The `id` of the control this label names. Required for the same reason Link's `href` is: a label with no `for` is a mistake the compiler catches, and passing `""` explicitly is the visible way to say "decorative label".  Named `for`, not `htmlFor`. Stencil maps a camelCase prop to its kebab attribute (`htmlFor` → `html-for`), so a consumer writing the HTML attribute `for` — the only spelling that exists in plain markup — would set nothing, and the label would silently associate with nothing. The first build proved it: `for="standalone-email"` in the page, `for=""` in the DOM. The native `for` attribute name is also what `Element.prototype` reserves, so a prop named `for` would collide with it — hence `for` as the *attribute* via `@Prop({ attribute: "for" })` on a differently-named field.

props.name: marker
props.description: Where the marker sits. `before` reads naturally for checkboxes and switches, where the control leads the sentence.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the labeled control as required and renders the marker.  This sets `aria-required` on **this** element, not the control — the consumer sets `required` on the control itself, and the label marking the control on its behalf would be a second component reaching into another's DOM, which §4 forbids.

ai.summary: A programmatic label for any control: names it through `for`, and clicking it focuses the control through the browser's own activation.
whenToUse: A control was built without its own label and needs one that is actually associated
A checkbox or switch needs its marker before the text, where the control leads the sentence
A custom field needs the same label record Input's built-in label uses
whenNotToUse: The control already has a label prop — Input and Textarea wire their own; two labels for one control is a bug
It would label nothing — `for` is required; a label with no control is a span with ambition, use plain text
The text describes a group of controls — use a Fieldset or a heading, not a label
ai.accessibility: Associates through `htmlFor` pointing at the control's id, so clicking the label focuses the control via the browser's own activation — no click handler here, because the platform's is better and reimplementing it means reimplementing its edge cases. The required marker is `aria-hidden`: the control's own `required` attribute carries the semantics, the asterisk is for the sighted, and color alone never carries it (WCAG 1.4.1). `required` here does not set anything on the control — a label reaching into another component's DOM is exactly what section 4 forbids.
knownLimitations: Field components render their control with the id `${hostId}-control`, so `for` must carry that suffix — a cross-component id contract is tracked as open
It cannot label a control rendered inside a shadow root it cannot see — `for` must match a light-DOM id
It does not generate ids; pair it with the control's own id or React's `useId()`

props.name: external
props.description: `external` marks a link that leaves the application: it adds the external icon, sets `target="_blank"`, and adds `rel="noopener noreferrer"`. Left off by default because most links do not leave.

props.name: href
props.description: The destination. A link that navigates.

props.name: rel
props.description: Forwarded to the underlying anchor.

props.name: subtle
props.description: Suppresses the underline until hover or focus.

props.name: target
props.description: Opens in a new tab without the external treatment.

ai.summary: Navigates to another URL, in place or in a new tab.
whenToUse: It changes the URL
The destination is a document or page
It can be opened in a new tab or copied by the reader
whenNotToUse: It performs an action without changing the URL — use a Button instead
It downloads a file rather than navigating — pass `download`
It triggers a dialog or menu — use a Button
ai.accessibility: Native anchor role, so middle-click, open-in-new-tab, and copy-link work. `external` sets target=_blank with rel=noopener noreferrer and renders a decorative indicator.
knownLimitations: An empty `href` renders as visibly disabled rather than failing at build time

props.name: label
props.description: The accessible name. Rendered as `aria-label` only when non-empty AND only when the host does not already carry `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`, because a consumer's own labelling must never be clobbered by a default.

props.name: max
props.description: The scale the value is measured against. Clamped to 0..max on render.

props.name: size
props.description: Track height scale.

props.name: value
props.description: The current value. A finite number makes the bar determinate; an absent (or non-finite) value makes it indeterminate — there is no honest percentage to report for a task whose length is unknown, so the contract says the bar sweeps instead of filling.

ai.summary: Shows how far along a task is, or that a task is running with no known end.
whenToUse: Work is in progress and the user is waiting on it
The completion fraction is known and moving
The progress explains why something else on the page is unavailable
whenNotToUse: The operation finished and its result is what matters — use an Alert
A single unmeasured delay is all there is — use a Spinner
It is a placeholder for content that is about to arrive — use a Skeleton
ai.accessibility: `role="progressbar"` with `aria-valuemin` and `aria-valuemax`, and `aria-valuenow` only when the value is determinate — an indeterminate bar that announced a number would be lying. The bar's width is derived from value over max. The `label` prop becomes `aria-label` only when the consumer set none of its own.
knownLimitations: No percentage text is rendered: formatting a number for the reader's locale is an Intl decision this element does not make
Under reduced motion the indeterminate bar keeps a static partial fill rather than sitting at zero, because an empty track reads as not started rather than unknown

ai.summary: An exclusive choice from a small set of options, rendered as real native radios so the browser owns arrow-key navigation and validation.
whenToUse: Exactly one choice from 2–7 known options
The options are short enough to read at a glance — longer lists want a Select
It must submit through a plain `<form>` with no JavaScript state
whenNotToUse: More than roughly 7 options — use a Select, which scrolls and filters
Several choices at once — use a Checkbox per option
A single on/off setting that acts immediately — use a Switch
ai.accessibility: Renders real native `<input type="radio">` elements in a `role="radiogroup"` container, so the browser owns arrow-key navigation within the group, the single tab stop, and constraint validation ("please select one of these options" is the browser's message, not a reimplementation). The group label names the container through `aria-labelledby`; each option is labelled by its wrapping label. An error sets `aria-invalid` and renders an icon beside its text, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1). Implements the FACE contract on the group: formResetCallback, formDisabledCallback, formStateRestoreCallback, and sk-value-change fires only for user-initiated changes.
knownLimitations: Options arrive as JSON, like Select — they cannot be slotted as children, because scoped encapsulation cannot distribute host children into the render tree
The generated `id` for the group label differs from React's `useId()`, so an SSR consumer must pass an explicit `id` (section 4, forms contract)

ai.summary: A real native <select>, visibly: submits through a plain form, validates natively, and the popup is the browser's own.
whenToUse: The value is one of a fixed set of choices
The form must submit through plain HTML with no component state reading
The list is long enough that radio buttons would be a wall
whenNotToUse: The choice is between two options — use a Switch or two Radio Buttons; a select hides the answer
The options depend on typing — use a Combobox
There are fewer than five options and the page has room — Radio Group shows every answer at once
ai.accessibility: Renders a real native `<select>`, visibly — §4's hidden-native path was rejected deliberately, so the popup is the browser's: touch, wheel, typeahead, and native validation all work without a listbox reimplementing them. FACE with all three form callbacks; `required` is enforced by the browser and never suppressed; the label is associated through `for`, and an error sets `aria-invalid` with an icon beside its text, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1). `sk-value-change` fires only for user-initiated changes. Options are JSON, because slot distribution cannot move host children into the render tree.
ai.example: <sk-select name="environment" label="Environment" required placeholder="Choose an environment" options='[{"value":"production","label":"Production"}]'></sk-select>
knownLimitations: The popup cannot be styled — that is the trade the visible-native decision makes, and it is why the popup works everywhere
Options are JSON, not slotted markup — slot distribution cannot reach the render tree
SSR consumers must pass an explicit `id` for a separately-rendered `Label` to find it (section 4, forms contract)

props.name: decorative
props.description: Purely visual: removes the element from the accessibility tree. Set it whenever the surrounding structure — a heading, whitespace, a card boundary — already communicates the break.

props.name: label
props.description: Label for a meaningful separator, e.g. "or" between two actions. Announced only when the separator is not decorative, because a name on a `role="none"` element is a contradiction.

props.name: orientation
props.description: Axis of the line. Vertical separators need a sized parent.

ai.summary: A hairline between content: a real <hr> that announces itself unless it is purely visual.
whenToUse: Two groups of content need a thematic break between them
A form's sections need dividing without a heading
A vertical rule splits two columns
whenNotToUse: The break is already communicated by a heading or Card boundary — mark it `decorative` or skip it
You are separating items in a list — use spacing or a list style; it is the honest tool
Two routes branch at a choice — use Tabs or a Radio Group to express the choice; "or" between buttons is not a widget
ai.accessibility: Renders a real `<hr>`, announced as a separator by screen readers. `decorative` flips it to `role="none"` for lines that exist only for the eye. A `label` (e.g. "or" between two actions) is announced only when the separator is meaningful — a name on a `role="none"` element is a contradiction. The line is the 1px hairline token, not the 3px chrome stroke: a separator divides content, and a 3px stroke between paragraphs reads as a wall.
knownLimitations: Vertical separators need a sized parent — `align-self: stretch` is the default, not a guarantee
No motion, no chrome, by design — the one component where the hairline is the point

ai.summary: A settings form grouping account fields, a select, switches, and a checkbox, with a save action and an inline alert.
whenToUse: A preferences or account screen where the grouping and the save affordance are the work
You want the label, description, and error wiring for each field already correct
whenNotToUse: A single field — use Input with a Label
A multi-step flow — the block is one form and no wizard state
ai.accessibility: Every control is a labelled `<sk-input>`, `<sk-select>`, `<sk-switch>`, or `<sk-checkbox>`; the switches are named by the visible label and explained by the description text beside them rather than by a title attribute. The alert is a live region, so a validation message is announced when it appears. The save button is a real `<button type="submit">`, so Enter in a field submits the form.
knownLimitations: The form has no validation logic and no submit handler: the values are markup, not state
Saving is not implemented — the button is a submit button waiting for the consumer's handler

props.name: direction
props.description: The shimmer's direction. Reversed for a right-to-left reading context, set by the consumer because the component does not know its locale.

props.name: variant
props.description: The shape being promised. `text` is a full-width line with the body line height, `circle` is a square bounding box with the full radius (a shape, not a style — same ruling as the Badge dot), `rect` is whatever box the consumer sizes.

ai.summary: A grey placeholder in the shape of content that is loading, so the page does not shift when the content arrives.
whenToUse: Content is loading into a known layout and the space must be held
A list, table, or card grid is fetching and the shape of what arrives is already known
whenNotToUse: An operation's duration matters — use a Spinner or Progress
The placeholder would be on screen more than a moment or two — show a real empty state instead
ai.accessibility: `aria-hidden` by design: a skeleton is scaffolding, not content, and announcing five grey rectangles before a table loads is noise. There is no `label` prop on purpose — if a region needs announcing while it loads, that is a live region and the consumer owns it. Real content announces itself when it arrives. Dimensions are the feature: every variant sets a default size the consumer overrides, because a skeleton that guesses the content's height causes the very layout shift it exists to prevent. Under reduced motion the shimmer is removed entirely rather than slowed — a slower shimmer is still motion, and the grey shape is the whole message.
knownLimitations: No slot by design: real content replaces the element, not its children
`direction` is a prop, not auto-detected — the component does not know its locale

props.name: label
props.description: What the wait is, announced to screen readers in place of the silent ring. "Loading" is the honest default; "Saving draft…" is the better one.

props.name: size
props.description: Ring diameter, from the icon-size tokens so the spinner matches the icon beside it. Not the `size` prop's height scale: a spinner is a circle, and a circle's size is its diameter.

props.name: status
props.description: Announces progress when it is known, e.g. "Uploading 60%".

ai.summary: A spinning ring for an operation in progress, announced to screen readers by its label rather than by the moving picture.
whenToUse: An operation is running and the interface cannot say how far along it is
A button or icon button is in its loading state and needs an inline indicator
whenNotToUse: Progress is measurable — use a Progress bar; a spinner cannot say 60%
Content is loading into a known layout — use a Skeleton, which promises the layout instead of motion
ai.accessibility: Carries `role="status"` so screen readers announce it as a live region. The visible ring is `aria-hidden` — it is a picture of waiting, and `label` (default "Loading") is what gets announced; `status` replaces it when progress is known. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` the spin stops rather than slows: a slow spinner still implies movement it cannot show, so the ring freezes solid and the label carries the whole story. Same ruling as Icon Button's loading state — if one changes, both must.
knownLimitations: It cannot express progress fraction — that is a Progress bar's job, not a faster spin

props.name: checked
props.description: Whether the switch is on. An ARIA-mirroring boolean, so the ARIA name verbatim (ADR-013, decision 1) — not `isOn`.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.description: Initial state for the uncontrolled case.

props.name: description
props.description: Persistent helper text below the row.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables interaction. Mirrors the ARIA name.

props.name: error
props.description: The validation message. Its presence drives `aria-invalid`.

props.name: form
props.description: Associates the control with a form it is not nested inside.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Marks the field invalid, with the same independence from `error` as Checkbox.

props.name: label
props.description: The label text, rendered beside the track. Wraps the control.

props.name: required
props.description: Native constraint validation still applies and is never suppressed.

props.name: size
props.description: Label text size. The row target stays 44px at every size.

props.name: value
props.description: The submitted value when on. `"on"` is the platform default, kept so a plain form reads exactly what a native checkbox-role=switch would send.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.

props.name: name
props.description: The name of the element, used when submitting an HTML form.

ai.summary: An on/off control that acts immediately, rendered as a native checkbox carrying role=switch so the browser keeps validation and form submission.
whenToUse: The setting applies the moment it is toggled — a preference, a visibility toggle
The state is genuinely binary: on or off, with no third state
It must submit through a plain `<form>` with no JavaScript state
whenNotToUse: The choice is collected for a later submit — use a Checkbox
The choice is one of several exclusive options — use a Radio Group
The action triggers something rather than setting a state — use a Button
ai.accessibility: Renders a real native `<input type="checkbox">` carrying `role="switch"`, so the browser supplies constraint validation, Space-to-toggle, and autofill while assistive technology reads the state as on/off. The label wraps the input, making the whole row the activation target with no click handler. `label`, `description`, and `error` are wired through the wrapping label and `aria-describedby`; an error sets `aria-invalid` and renders an icon beside its text, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1). Implements the FACE contract: formResetCallback, formDisabledCallback, formStateRestoreCallback, and sk-value-change fires only for user-initiated changes.
knownLimitations: The generated `id` for the inner control differs from React's `useId()`, so an SSR consumer must pass an explicit `id` for a separately-rendered `Label` to find it (section 4, forms contract)

props.name: density
props.description: Cell padding, not a height scale. `size` is the height scale every other component uses and a table has no intrinsic height — it is whatever its rows make it. Density is the axis a table actually varies on, and its default value is named for what it is rather than for a comfort level: `default` matches `variant`, and a table that wants tighter rows opts in.

props.name: label
props.description: The name of the scroll region.  The viewport is focusable (`tabindex="0"`) because a scrollable region that cannot be reached from the keyboard is unreachable content (WCAG 2.1.1). With a label it also carries `role="group"` and an accessible name; with none it carries no role at all — an unnamed group is noise in the accessibility tree, not structure.

props.name: striped
props.description: Zebra rows: even body rows take the sunken surface.

props.name: variant
props.description: `default` is the stroked, shadowed container; `plain` drops the container chrome for a table sitting inside a `sk-card`.

ai.summary: A styled container for tabular data, which the consumer writes as a real table.
whenToUse: Tabular data where comparison down a column is the point
The same data in a narrow viewport must scroll sideways without breaking the page
The table needs the dense or striped treatment without hand-rolling it
whenNotToUse: It is a read-only summary of a few fields — use a Card
The layout is a grid of unrelated panels — use Cards in a layout primitive
There is one column and no comparison to make — use a list of Text rows
ai.accessibility: The consumer writes the semantics: `<caption>`, `<thead>`, and `<th scope>`. This element adds a scrollable region that is reachable from the keyboard and carries `role="group"` with an accessible name only when `label` is set — a scroll region a keyboard user cannot reach hides its own content. `label` names that region; it is not a substitute for a `<caption>`.

knownLimitations: It does not sort, paginate, or read the rows: the table inside is the consumer's markup
Sticky headers are not implemented — the scroll height belongs to the consumer's own container, so a sticky offset this element chose would be wrong

props.name: active
props.description: The active tab's index. Zero-based, over the tabs in DOM order.

props.name: label
props.description: The tab's label. A consumer may instead slot rich content.

props.name: hidden
props.description: Panels start hidden; the widget reveals the active one.

ai.summary: Roving-tabindex tabs: the tablist owns the keyboard, arrows move and activate, and the active panel is the only one rendered.
whenToUse: Related content shares one surface and only one view matters at a time
The views are peers — Settings-style sections, editor panes
Switching should feel like moving, not navigating
whenNotToUse: Each view is a destination — use navigation, not tabs
The views must be compared side by side — show them all
Content must stay mounted across switches — this component unmounts inactive panels
ai.accessibility: The ARIA tabs pattern's hard rule is enforced: only the active tab is in the tab order, arrow keys move and activate (automatic activation), Home and End jump to the ends, and activation wraps. Tabs are real `<button>`s. `aria-selected` / `aria-controls` / `aria-labelledby` are computed and written by the widget, because tabs and panels are separately slotted. Arrow semantics derive from `getComputedStyle().direction` at interaction time, so `dir="rtl"` inverts Left and Right with no build flag (§4). The active panel carries `tabindex=0` so keyboard users reach its content after the last tab.
ai.example:

Billing history.
knownLimitations: Inactive panels are hidden, not kept alive — state inside a panel is lost on switch, unless the application holds it
The tablist slot must carry `data-slot="tablist"` and each part its `data-slot` — the wiring contract is structural

props.name: family
props.description: Which family to set. The default leaves `font-family` untouched, because body copy inherits the platform stack and re-declaring it per-element would fight any consumer who changes `--sk-font-body`.

props.name: muted
props.description: Muted text. The one color decision a text component owns, because secondary text is a *typographic* role in this system — it exists as `.sk-text-muted` today, and this is where that class retires to.

props.name: variant
props.description: The type step to apply, named exactly as the token is.  This is the `variant` slot of the §4 two-prop rule — the axis a text component varies on. `size` is not used for it, because `size` is the height scale every other component uses and a text element has no height of its own to scale.

ai.summary: Applies one whole type step — size, line-height, weight, and tracking together — to any element.
whenToUse: A heading, paragraph, or label must match the type scale without hand-assembling four tokens
The consumer's markup chooses the element; the look must come from the system
Display-face headings at weight 800, or muted secondary text
whenNotToUse: Text inside a Button or Card heading slot — those components already apply their own steps
You want to choose the element with a prop — pick the element in markup instead; an `as` prop is how heading levels end up contradicting the outline
Text that is a control — a link is a Link, not styled text
ai.accessibility: Renders no wrapper and no role: the element the consumer chose keeps its semantics, and the component only sets typography. There is no `as` prop by design — an element-choosing prop invites `<h3 as="h2">`-style fixes that contradict the document outline. `muted` sets color only; the muted pair passes the contrast gates in both themes (6.64:1 light).
knownLimitations: There is no `size` prop: `size` is the height scale other components use, and text has no intrinsic height — `variant` names the type step instead
It does not truncate, clamp, or balance lines — layout concerns stay with the consumer

props.name: cols
props.description: Visible columns, for the few cases where it matters.

props.name: defaultValue
props.description: Initial value for the uncontrolled case.

props.name: description
props.description: Persistent helper text below the field.

props.name: disabled
props.description: Disables interaction. Mirrors the ARIA name.

props.name: error
props.description: The validation message. Its presence drives `aria-invalid`.

props.name: form
props.description: Associates the control with a form it is not nested inside.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Marks the field invalid independently of any error text.

props.name: label
props.description: The control's own label text, rendered above the field.

props.name: maxLength
props.description: Maximum accepted length, enforced natively. Same attribute-name reason.

props.name: minLength
props.description: Minimum accepted length, enforced natively.  Attribute-observed because Stencil's camelCase-to-kebab mapping produces `min-length`, not the native `minlength`, so `<sk-textarea minlength="2">` was silently ignored — the same class of defect `readonly` had.

props.name: placeholder
props.description: Placeholder text. Never a substitute for a label.

props.name: readOnly
props.description: Makes the field non-editable but still submitted and focusable.  Attribute-observed, for the same reason as `sk-input`: Stencil's camelCase-to-kebab mapping produces `read-only`, not the native `readonly`.

props.name: required
props.description: Native constraint validation still applies and is never suppressed.

props.name: rows
props.description: Visible rows. The browser's own sizing, not a pixel value.

props.name: value
props.description: The value. Uncontrolled by default: typed value only if set.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual emphasis.

props.name: name
props.description: The name of the element, used when submitting an HTML form.

ai.summary: A multi-line text field that participates in a plain HTML form, for text too long to type on one line.
whenToUse: The value runs to several lines: a bio, a comment, release notes, an address
The consumer wants the browser to size the field by line count
It must submit through a plain `<form>` with no JavaScript state
whenNotToUse: The value is a single short string — use an Input
The value is one of a fixed set — use a Select or Radio Group
It only toggles a boolean — use a Checkbox or Switch
ai.accessibility: Renders a real native `<textarea>`, so the browser supplies constraint validation and the error bubble rather than this component reimplementing them. `label`, `description`, and `error` are wired through `<label for>` and `aria-describedby`; an error sets `aria-invalid` and renders an icon beside its text, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1). The field resizes vertically by default, because long-form text is edited rather than typed in one line. Shares its form contract with Input.
knownLimitations: There is no `pattern` prop: a textarea has no single-line grammar for a pattern to constrain
The generated `id` for the inner control differs from React's `useId()`, so an SSR consumer must pass an explicit `id` for a separately-rendered `Label` to find it (section 4, forms contract)

props.name: duration
props.description: Milliseconds before auto-dismiss. `0` never auto-dismisses — for an error the user must act on, an expiring message is an expired apology.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the toast is showing.

props.name: variant
props.description: Visual severity, matching Badge's palette. Color is never the message.

ai.summary: A non-blocking notification on the glass material: announced politely, auto-dismissed, never stealing focus.
whenToUse: A background operation finished and the user was looking somewhere else
A state change should be acknowledged without interrupting work
An error needs time and a close button, not a decision
whenNotToUse: The user must choose before the page continues — use an Alert Dialog
The message needs the page's context hidden — use a Dialog
The information is permanent UI, not an event — use a Card or a Badge
ai.accessibility: `role="status"`, a polite live region: announced when it appears, never stealing focus — the user was looking somewhere else, and a toast that shouts is a dialog wearing a smaller skirt. Hover or focus pauses the auto-dismiss clock, because a message that disappears mid-read is an announcement that never happened. `duration=0` never expires: an error the user must act on deserves more than an expired apology. The close button carries a real `aria-label` — a bare × is a picture to a screen reader. Severity is a 3px left edge plus the message text, never color alone (WCAG 1.4.1).
knownLimitations: It is a single toast — the consumer's region owns stacking and placement
It never takes focus, so keyboard users meet it only through announcement; an actionable toast needs a persistent surface

props.name: delay
props.description: Milliseconds of hover before showing. A tooltip that fires instantly is a strobe.

props.name: open
props.description: Whether the tooltip is showing. Driven by hover/focus; also settable.

props.name: placement
props.description: Preferred side. Flips at the viewport edge rather than clipping.

ai.summary: A short description of something the user can already see: shows on hover and keyboard focus, announced on demand via aria-describedby.
whenToUse: An icon-only control needs its name spelled out
A jargon term or abbreviation needs one sentence of context
A control is disabled and the reason helps
whenNotToUse: The information is essential — put it in the page; a tooltip hides it from touch and from anyone not hovering
The content is interactive or long — use a Popover
It is the control's name — use a Label or aria-label; a tooltip is a description, not the name
ai.accessibility: Named through `aria-describedby` pointing at the panel, so a screen reader reads it on demand — a tooltip that grabs focus is a popup wearing a tiny hat. Shows on hover after a delay (a tooltip that fires instantly is a strobe) and immediately on keyboard focus, because a tabbing user asked for it explicitly and a 300ms penance on every tab is hostile. Escape hides it. The panel takes no pointer events (`pointer-events: none`), so hovering the tooltip never flickers it away. Explicitly excluded from the forms contract (section 4): it cannot be form-associated.
ai.example:
<sk-tooltip placement="top">
  <sk-button slot="trigger">Deploy</sk-button>
  Ships the current build to production.
</sk-tooltip>
knownLimitations: Placement is a hint, not a viewport-aware computation — the panel anchors to the trigger and can clip at edges
Touch has no hover: a tooltip is invisible on touch until the control is focused
The trigger must be a focusable element — a non-interactive span gives keyboard users nothing to describe
